sections.html: Jefferson County is a rural Big Bend county of about 14,000 people, with Monticello as the county seat, 25 miles east of Tallahassee. Farms, ranches and timberland cover most of it. A town lot in Monticello, a farm parcel in the north and a coastal tract do not sit in the same taxing districts, so two Jefferson County bills rarely look alike.

sections.h2: Who sends and who reads a Jefferson County tax bill
sections.html:
Three independent offices share the work. The county's website points residents to jeffersonpa.net for parcel search and exemption filing.

  • Property Appraiser: sets the assessed value and takes exemption applications.
  • Tax Collector: mails statements on or before November 1, accepts payment and runs the certificate sale.
  • Clerk and Comptroller: keeps official records and conducts a tax deed auction if one is requested.

Every August the appraiser mails a TRIM notice showing the parcel's value and the rates each taxing body proposes. The hearings listed on it take place before rates are set in September.

Six lines appear on the Tax Collector's millage list. A house inside Monticello sees all six, while a rural parcel skips the city line. One mill is one-tenth of a cent, or a dollar per thousand of taxable value.

The commissioners, the school board, the city council and the two water districts each vote on their own rate. Charges for services appear apart from these lines, so ask the collector which ones apply at your address.

sections.h2: What does the calendar look like from November to June?
sections.html:
Statements must be mailed by November 1. An early payer saves 4 percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. After that the clock runs toward April.

  • April 1: unpaid real estate tax is delinquent and takes a 3 percent penalty.
  • Early May: unpaid accounts are advertised in the local paper.
  • By June 1: the online certificate sale.

Tangible personal property, such as business equipment, draws a 1.5 percent monthly penalty once it is late. A year's lien attaches at the start of that year.

Homestead can cut $50,000 from the taxable figure. The first $25,000 applies to every levy, and the second $25,000 spares school levies. Send Form DR-501 to the appraiser before the March 1 cutoff for a house that was your permanent home on January 1. Renting the house or moving out ends the exemption.

An income-tested senior add-on worth as much as $50,000 exists only where the local government chose to adopt it. Disabled veteran and deployed servicemember benefits are also listed by the state. Ask the Jefferson County Property Appraiser which local options are in force. Annual growth in a homestead's assessed value is capped, and that cushion ends at a sale.

sections.h2: Does land use affect a Jefferson County sale?
sections.html:
It can. Building in the county is a two-step process: a Development Permit from the Planning Department first, then building permits from the Building Department. No building permit is issued for a site without the first. Land Development Regulations reach every kind of development, including driveways and power poles.

Any subdivision of land needs approval under the Land Development Code, and that approval should be confirmed before new deeds are recorded. If land is conveyed without it, later owners may be unable to get a building permit. A seller splitting off acreage should settle this before a buyer's attorney raises it.

  • Older and historic structures raise their own questions at sale time, such as roof age, wiring and flood zone. FEMA's Flood Map Service Center, which the county links, shows the zone for a given parcel.
  • The county holds a Community Rating System score of 8 under the federal flood insurance program, which earns premium discounts.

sections.h2: Handling the tax balance as a seller
sections.html:
The seller carries the tax up to the closing date, and older unpaid years must be cleared for clean title. The closing agent normally requests a payoff from the collector and pays it at the table from the seller's side.

The roll is a working roll and amounts can change during the year, so any quote is only a snapshot. Get the payoff in writing with a date near closing. If an escrowing lender holds your money, ask how soon any leftover balance returns.

  • Search the parcel on the collector's site and note every year with a balance.
  • Ask whether a certificate was sold, since redemption takes certified funds.
  • Confirm exemptions with the appraiser so the title company prorates correctly.
  • The clerk records the deed and takes the stamp tax at the counter.

Bring your parcel number and a copy of your deed when you contact an office. A buyer paying cash has no lender appraisal or underwriting to wait for, so a back-tax payoff can be taken from your proceeds without delaying the closing.

sections.h2: Before you list a Jefferson County property
sections.html:
A little groundwork keeps a sale on schedule. Start by pulling your parcel record and your latest tax statement, and check that the owner name and legal description match your deed. Next, ask the Tax Collector whether any earlier year still shows a balance. Then talk to the Property Appraiser about whether your exemptions will end at closing and how that affects the split between you and the buyer.

If you plan to sell part of a larger tract, settle the subdivision question with the Planning Department first. Rural parcels with wells, septic systems or old outbuildings may also draw questions from a buyer's inspector, so gather permits and receipts you already have. A sale to a cash buyer skips the mortgage appraisal step, which can help when a parcel is unusual or has paperwork gaps, though the title company still needs a clean record.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Jefferson County tax?
sections.html:
The debt is sold to an investor as a certificate. The collector describes it as a lien created by paying the delinquent tax, not a purchase of the property. The sale is a reverse auction on interest that starts at 18 percent, and the lowest bidder wins.

Certificates last seven years, and the face amount includes the 3 percent penalty, a 5 percent collector's commission and advertising costs. A homestead whose face value is under $250 is issued to the county at 18 percent instead of being sold. If the 22 month period runs out, the parcel can go to a tax deed sale, which the clerk runs after the holder applies once two years have gone by. The opening bid on a homestead includes half the latest assessed value. A March 31 deferral application date may help an owner at risk.

faqs.q: When does unpaid Jefferson County real estate tax turn delinquent?
faqs.a: April 1, when a 3 percent penalty lands. The local paper runs unpaid accounts in early May, and the online certificate sale follows by June 1.

faqs.q: What discount do I get for paying a Jefferson County bill early?
faqs.a: Four percent in November, 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. Statements are mailed on or before November 1.

faqs.q: Is the Monticello millage line on every Jefferson County bill?
faqs.a: No. The 2026 list has a separate Monticello line of .00685010, which applies to parcels inside the city only.

faqs.q: Can I build on Jefferson County land without a permit?
faqs.a: No. The county requires a Development Permit from Planning first, then building permits, and subdivisions need approval before new deeds are recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I file for homestead in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: At the appraiser's office or on jeffersonpa.net, using Form DR-501, before March 1.
